item.title: Quantum-Inspired Risk Portfolio Optimization via Exponential Tilting
item.description: arXiv:2611.27990v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Financial portfolio optimization is often framed through mean-variance objectives, yet real profit-and-loss (P&L) scenario distributions are typically discrete and non-Gaussian. To explore realistic P&L distributions, we propose an objective function based on exponential tilting and certainty equivalent under constant absolute risk aversion. We then derive a second-order approximation, recovering a quadratic optimization problem solvable through mixed integer quadratic programming (MIQP) and quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO). Constraints in the QUBO formulation are incorporated via Lagrangian relaxation and slack variable approaches, enabling a direct comparison between classical constrained MIQP and quantum-inspired methods. In order to study how exponential tilting affects mean, standard deviation, and tail-risk measures such as Value at Risk and Conditional Value at Risk, we design an experimental protocol based on scanning a grid of tilt parameters and solving the associated optimization problems. The results on a realistic trading portfolio show how the tilts can be tuned to optimize different risk-return profiles while remaining competitive with those found using other state-of-the-art approaches. Moreover, performance analysis suggests that, even using classical solvers, the QUBO formulation with Lagrangian relaxation scales better than the MIQP approach, providing the best constraint encoding strategy.

item.title: Gated Payoff-Weighted Net Profit Maximization For Online Portfolio Selection With Transaction Costs
item.description: arXiv:2611.29552v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study online portfolio selection (OLPS) problems. The net profit maximization (NPM) acting upon Adaptive Online Moving Average (AOLMA), namely the AOLNPM strategy in portfolio selection, trades when forecast gain exceeds the transaction cost. In essence, this method relies heavily on calibrated forecasts. Indeed, we show that AOLMA forecasts overstate the realized relative returns. We therefore design a gate that adjusts how strongly an AOLMA forecast is used; for each asset, it learns the recent mixture proportion assigned to AOLMA from predictive likelihoods against a neutral forecast (no change). The proportion therefore estimates the extent to which the forecast is realized. We then feed the resulting forecast into the NPM portfolio rule, where the gate acts as an asset-specific cost threshold. A payoff-weighted fund combines gated NPM experts with fixed decay factors in proportion to their wealth and needs no learning rate. On nine datasets with a transaction cost rate of 0.1%, our method produces 5.9 times the wealth of AOLNPM in geometric mean and sits above AOLNPM on every dataset, with its preponderance growing with the cost rate.
item.dc:creator: Grace Chengrong Xie, Alvey Qianli Lin, Wai Ki Ching

item.title: Cleaning correlation matrices with external information: the Maximum Variance estimat
item.description: arXiv:2611.30843v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rotationally invariant estimators clean the eigenvalues of an empirical correlation matrix but keep its noisy eigenvectors. We study an estimator that corrects the eigenvectors by using external information, namely a partition of the assets into groups such as asset classes or regions. The Maximum Variance (MaxVar) estimator restricts the leading eigenvectors to linear combinations of the maximum-variance portfolios of the groups and replaces the rest of the spectrum by a single eigenvalue. It is a factor model with about n parameters instead of n2/2, and it is positive de nite even when the number of observations is smaller than the number of assets n. We apply it to the correlation matrix of 47 futures on stock indices, bonds and currencies, with the three asset classes as groups. In an illustrative Monte Carlo test, in which the reference matrix has the structure assumed by the estimator, the distance to the reference is reduced by one third with respect to the empirical matrix, against less than 10% for the rotationally invariant estimator. The decisive test is the performance of a portfolio on real data: over 1993-2018, the Sharpe ratio of the risk parity portfolio, which involves the inverse of the matrix, is 1.28 with the MaxVar estimator, 1.24 with the rotationally invariant estimator and 1.17 with the empirical matrix, and the advantage increases when the estimation window is shortened.
item.dc:creator: S\'ebastien Valeyre

item.title: Per-Prediction Uncertainty Is Not a Regime Detector: A Detectability Bound and Two-Level Deployment for Cross-Sectional Equity Rankers
item.description: arXiv:2611.27992v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Quantitative finance is increasingly exploring AI-native and agent-mediated allocation: when should an allocator trust a cross-sectional ranker after a silent regime shift that volatility controls miss? Aleatoric scaling addresses market noise; it does not detect epistemic invalidity when ranking structure breaks without a volatility footprint. Building on Sanderink (2026), "When Alpha Breaks" (arXiv:2603.13252), which established per-stock epistemic uncertainty, rank-geometry coupling, and a two-level gate on a walk-forward LightGBM US AI-exposure panel, this paper asks whether per-stock scores can be pooled into portfolio-wide health, or whether strategy-level abstention must condition on realised outcomes. RQ1 (Separation): Does epistemic uncertainty capture model-specific failure distinct from volatility? RQ2 (Decision value): Does a two-level architecture beat baselines on risk-adjusted return and drawdown? RQ3 (Robustness): Do answers hold across regimes, a second ranker, falsification tests, and a universe-readiness gate? We prove a detectability bound: score-only aggregates of per-prediction error predictors cannot beat chance under strict concept shift. CIFAR-10-C confirms the covariate-versus-concept dichotomy (AUROC 0.955 vs 0.500); equity cross-sectional aggregates stay near chance (bad-day AUROC ~0.55) despite valid per-stock signals. The constructive escape is Y-conditioning: partial-horizon RankIC CUSUM (k=5; AUROC 0.796) and a matured-RankIC regime-trust index. Falsification tests and a universe-readiness stop verdict bound allocator claims. Rank-geometry coupling (rho=0.616) forces a discrete tail-cap and strategy gate. Evidence is historical walk-forward simulation on one thematic universe (N<=100) through February 2025; the validated object is reliability architecture, not transportable alpha.
item.dc:creator: Ursina Sanderink

item.title: Do Candlestick Charts Suffice? The Incremental Economic Value of Technical Indicators in Stock Return Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2611.30584v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Although technical analysis remains widely used in practice, the need for manually constructed indicators is increasingly questioned as deep learning models can extract features directly from OHLC price data. This paper examines the standalone economic value of trading volume and manually constructed technical-indicator groups and whether adding these groups to OHLC candlestick charts provides incremental economic value. Using daily data for 1,707 Chinese A-share stocks from 2013 to 2025, we construct approximately 3.36 million stock-window samples and encode them as multi-channel images containing candlestick charts, trading volume, and seven widely used manually constructed technical indicators. The primary analysis uses a 2D CNN on these images; complementary tests apply a logistic regression, a 1D CNN, and an LSTM to numerical representations of the same samples. Out-of-sample performance from 2021 to 2025 is evaluated using decile portfolios, Sharpe ratios, Fama--French alphas, and formal pairwise tests. Our empirical results yield two central findings. First, specifications based separately on OHLC, trading volume, and each technical-indicator group produce significantly positive high-minus-low returns and factor-adjusted alphas, together with economically meaningful Sharpe ratios; the OHLC-only specifications generally perform best under the nonlinear models. Second, adding these technical-indicator groups to OHLC does not systematically improve any of these performance measures in our setting. Together, these results provide the first large-scale evidence from the Chinese A-share market on the standalone and incremental economic value of these technical-indicator groups across multiple representations and model architectures.
item.dc:creator: Peng Liu, Yanyan Zheng
